items.stem: A payments risk lead must approve how the fraud-review threshold is tuned before checkout rollout. A false rejection blocks a legitimate customer's payment; a missed fraud case is caught and reversed the next business day. Which threshold policy should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Return to discovery to re-price both error directions before making any threshold decision.
Optimize the model for the highest overall accuracy across both error types on the evaluation set.
Bias the threshold toward recall and route flagged cases to human review before blocking any payment.
Bias the threshold toward precision, accepting more missed fraud cases to avoid blocking legitimate payments.

items.whyRight: The false rejection is irreversible at the moment of checkout, while a missed fraud case is caught and reversed the next day; the threshold should minimize the costlier, unrecoverable error rather than treat both directions as equally acceptable.

whyWrong.A: The stem already prices both directions — irreversible versus next-day recoverable — so returning to discovery discards evidence already given instead of acting on it.
whyWrong.B: A flat accuracy target weights both error directions equally, but the stem states one direction is irreversible and the other recoverable.
whyWrong.C: This directly increases the false-rejection rate, which the stem already establishes as the irreversible, costlier error — the opposite of what the stated asymmetry requires.

items.t1Clause: a missed fraud case is caught and reversed the next business day
items.factAnswerRaw: Bias toward precision; set a higher action threshold

items.stem: A CFO is deciding whether to renew a document-processing contract and needs a defensible number before the board meeting. The architect currently declines to quote any accuracy figure, citing wide variance across document types. What should the architect do instead?

opts.t: Report figures segmented by document type, the measurement method, and the end-to-end outcome including human review.
Report a single blended accuracy figure, since it is honest given the stated method and evaluation set.
Report only the underlying model's classification accuracy, since that is the metric the CFO originally asked about.
Decline to provide any figure until the sponsor accepts that accuracy depends on document type.

items.whyRight: The CFO has a budget decision to make and cannot make it on a qualitative answer; segmented figures with the measurement basis and end-to-end outcome, including the human-review step, give a defensible number to plan against.

whyWrong.B: The stem states performance varies sharply by document type, so a single blended figure is contradicted by the evidence already given, not merely imprecise.
whyWrong.C: This states a real figure but omits the human-review step and the end-to-end outcome, which is what the CFO's budget decision actually depends on.
whyWrong.D: The CFO's renewal decision needs a number to plan against; declining to quantify is not acceptable even though the underlying variability claim is true.

items.t1Clause: citing wide variance across document types

items.stem: After a polished pre-launch demo, a sponsor now assumes the system performs at that level for all incoming volume and is building next quarter's staffing plan on that assumption. What should the architect put in place before rollout?

opts.t: Establish a recurring review that reports real performance on real production inputs against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Send a detailed written memo to the sponsor explaining the system's real performance and current limitations.
Restructure users' ad hoc feedback into a structured log of input, output, expected output, and reviewer feeding the evaluation set.
Have the sponsor formally accept the demo's results as the system's expected production baseline going forward.

items.whyRight: Expectations re-inflate after every demonstration, so a one-time correction cannot hold against continuous drift; only a recurring measurement against agreed criteria keeps the sponsor's plan anchored to real production performance rather than a single favorable demo.

whyWrong.B: A memo corrects today's understanding but expectations re-inflate at the next demonstration; the table treats a one-time correction as necessary, not sufficient, against continuous drift.
whyWrong.C: This is the right fix for scattered chat-channel complaints, but the stem describes overconfidence from a clean demo, not ungathered failure reports.
whyWrong.D: This locks in a single favorable measurement as a standing commitment instead of establishing the recurring review that continuous expectation drift actually requires.

items.factAnswerRaw: Establish a recurring review showing real performance on real inputs against the agreed criteria

items.stem: A model-tier decision was recorded a year ago under a strict latency ceiling that has since been relaxed by the platform team. The evaluation numbers and the rejected alternatives from that decision are unchanged. What should the architect check first?

opts.t: Schedule a walkthrough session where the original architects explain their reasoning to the questioning team.
Re-run the original latency and quality benchmark from scratch on the current infrastructure.
Move immediately to a higher-capability model, since the ceiling that constrained the original choice no longer applies.
Retrieve the decision record's stated constraint and re-evaluate the original trade-off now that the ceiling has moved.

items.whyRight: The record exists for exactly this moment: when a driving constraint changes, checking what was recorded against the new condition is the fastest way to tell whether the original decision still holds, before any component is re-built.

whyWrong.A: A walkthrough transfers the reasoning once to whoever attends, but it goes stale immediately and gives the team nothing durable to check the next time a constraint moves.
whyWrong.B: This discards a year of recorded evaluation numbers and rebuilds them before checking whether the ceiling change even affects the original trade-off.
whyWrong.C: This spends money on a capability upgrade before confirming, against the recorded trade-off, whether the relaxed ceiling actually changes which tier is warranted.

items.t1Clause: The evaluation numbers and the rejected alternatives from that decision are unchanged
items.factAnswerRaw: Check the recorded constraint and re-evaluate against it

items.stem: A successful pilot served 40 users: a 1-in-500 failure occurred twice across 200 cases, and human review absorbed 12% of pilot volume. Before recommending rollout to 800 users, which two points must the architect's report to sponsor leadership include?

opts.t: Rate limits and infrastructure capacity for 800-user volume are necessary and should headline the report as the binding constraint.
The report should recommend a higher-capability model ahead of rollout to preempt the wider input variety at scale.
The 1-in-500 failure rate should be planned for as a routine, several-times-daily event at full volume.
The 12% human-review load should be converted into a staffing line sized for 800-user volume.

items.whyRight: Both are pilot-to-scale assumptions that break at higher volume: a rare failure becomes routine at scale, and human review invisible in the pilot must become an explicit staffing line before the budget is approved by leadership.

whyWrong.A: Capacity planning is necessary but the table explicitly treats it as the visible constraint, not the binding one — the input-distribution risk is what actually determines whether rollout succeeds.
whyWrong.B: This spends on a bigger model before anyone has characterised the inputs at 800-user volume, skipping the assumption audit the report is meant to deliver.

items.t1Clause: human review absorbed 12% of pilot volume
